policy_title: Strengthen UK Defence and National Security
stated: Labour commits absolutely to the UK’s nuclear deterrent and maintains an unshakeable commitment to NATO, applying a NATO test to major defence programmes. The party will increase defence spending to 2.5% of GDP and conduct a Strategic Defence Review in its first year, adapting counter-terrorism approaches to state-based domestic security threats. This includes introducing 'Martyn's Law' for public venues and updating counter-extremism rules.

source.quote: Our commitment to the UK’s nuclear deterrent is absolute. It is a vital safeguard for the UK and our NATO allies. As the party that founded NATO, we maintain our unshakeable commitment to the alliance, and we will apply a NATO test to major defence programmes to ensure we meet our obligations in full. To ensure the UK is fully prepared to deal with these interconnected threats, Labour will conduct a Strategic Defence Review within our first year in government, and we will set out the path to spending 2.5 per cent of GDP on defence. Labour will take the approach used for dealing with non-state terrorism and adapt it to deal with state-based domestic security threats. Labour will bring in ‘Martyn’s Law’ to strengthen the security of public events and venues. We will update the rules around counter-extremism, including online, to stop people being radicalised and drawn towards hateful ideologies. Labour will also ensure the police and intelligence services have the powers and resources they need to protect the British people from terrorism and hostile espionage.

bearing_set.reason: Directly affects national security posture (nuclear deterrent, NATO, defence spending), counter-terrorism capacity, and public venue safety (Martyn's Law) — all core O5 indicators.

Martyn's Law imposes mandatory security requirements on public venues (state coercion/mandates on operators and potentially patrons), and updated counter-extremism rules could restrict speech and expression or expand surveillance — concrete mechanisms moving the 'freedom from state coercion' and 'freedom of speech' indicators.

Committing to raise defence spending from roughly 2–2.3% to 2.5% of GDP represents a material additional fiscal outlay (estimated ~£10–15bn/yr extra), which must be funded, borrowed, or offset — directly affecting the funded-vs-borrowed balance and debt-path sustainability indicators.

membership_note: Three fundamentals earn real verdicts: O5 (the policy's designed-for outcome), O10 (Martyn's Law mandates and counter-extremism rules impose coercive/regulatory obligations with a plausible liberty cost), and O12 (a significant new spending commitment materially affects public finances). Effects on O13 or O15 are too indirect and mechanism-thin to clear the non-negligible bar.
